top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B040) isolates one general mechanism: collateral-linked borrowing limits feed back on asset prices, so small shocks become large and persistent. It has about three decades of extension, criticism and use in macro-finance and policy models. Attribution is the cleanest on the slate, because the originating paper has two authors and no co-originator is left out under the three-name cap. I would word the citation around the mechanism and its influence, not around a settled size of amplification. The main costs are that direct empirical validation is indirect, the 2022 overlap is only narrowed, and leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist favours theory over tested evidence. I rank P002 (Autor, Dorn and Hanson, narrowed to the trade-shock evidence) second. It has strong direct identification and clean three-author attribution, but a shorter record and a continuing debate over shift-share inference and over trade versus automation. P003 (Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn) is a durable methodological advance but rests on functional-form and instrument assumptions. I rank it third, above no award, because all three proposals are credible, mature achievements.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; the profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn. My research is in economic history, outside these fields. My Lund colleague Tommy Andersson also supports P001, which is an institutional connection with a committee member and not a tie to any candidate.
